key_instruments: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689); amended by the 'Digital Omnibus on AI' (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
scope: all AI systems, with a risk-based tiering (banned practices, high-risk, limited-risk transparency duties, general-purpose AI models); binding across all 27 EU member states
enforcement_mechanism: yes — national market-surveillance authorities plus a new EU AI Office; fines up to 7% of global annual revenue (or €35m) for banned-practice violations, up to 3% for other breaches
effective_date_or_status: Entered into force 1 Aug 2024; banned practices + AI literacy rules applied from 2 Feb 2025; general-purpose AI model rules from 2 Aug 2025; Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) formally adopted by the Council 29 Jun 2026, published in the Official Journal 24 Jul 2026, entered into force 27 Jul 2026 — it pushes standalone high-risk (Annex III) system rules from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027, and high-risk systems embedded in regulated products (Annex I) from 2 Aug 2027 to 2 Aug 2028; Article 50 transparency/labeling duties (e.g. disclosing AI-generated content) are NOT delayed and remain effective 2 Aug 2026 (only the watermarking technical requirement for already-deployed systems gets a 4-month reprieve to 2 Dec 2026)
plain_language_summary: The EU is the first place in the world with a real, binding AI law. It bans a few dangerous uses of AI outright, and for 'high-risk' uses like hiring or credit-scoring tools, companies must test and register the systems before selling them. Fines for breaking the rules can reach 7% of a company's worldwide revenue. In mid-2026 the EU formally passed a 'Digital Omnibus' law that pushed the toughest high-risk-system deadlines back to December 2027 and August 2028 (from August 2026/2027) — but the requirement to label AI-generated content still starts in August 2026 as originally planned.
verification_notes: Agent 1's dates for prohibited practices (2 Feb 2025) and GPAI rules (2 Aug 2025) confirmed independently (Gibson Dunn, Cloud Security Alliance, DLA Piper all agree). Agent 1 flagged the post-Omnibus high-risk dates as unconfirmed against a primary source; I confirmed them: the Digital Omnibus on AI was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal 24 Jul 2026, in force 27 Jul 2026 (multiple independent law-firm trackers agree on this citation and on the Dec 2027/Aug 2028 dates, which happen to match the dates Agent 1 had already written). Added the important nuance Agent 1 lacked: Article 50 transparency/AI-content-labeling duties were NOT delayed and still start 2 Aug 2026 — only the harder Annex III/I high-risk obligations were pushed back. Upgraded confidence from medium to high given this is now confirmed against a specific, dated regulation.

Rather than fight it out in court, Colorado's legislature rewrote its own law in May 2026 into a much narrower, disclosure-focused version — so the 'who's really in charge' fight between states and the federal government is still playing out, but its most concrete effect so far has been to make Colorado's actual rules weaker than originally planned.
